title: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
summary: How data moves from HBM through L2 and L1 to registers, why a warp's loads are served in 32-byte sectors, how strides and misalignment waste bandwidth, and how shared memory tiles with padding fix a matrix transpose.
outcomes: Explain where registers, shared memory, L1, L2 and global memory live and who can see each
Compute the sectors per warp request and the fraction of bytes used for unit, strided and misaligned access
Compute theoretical and effective bandwidth and use them to judge a kernel
Compute the shared memory bank of each thread and the conflict degree for a given stride
Rewrite a strided kernel with a padded shared memory tile so that global and shared accesses are both efficient

lessons.title: From registers to HBM: the GPU memory map

blocks.md:
From the programming model course you know that a kernel runs as a grid of thread blocks, that each block runs on one **streaming multiprocessor** (SM), and that the SM executes threads in **warps** of 32. From the cache hierarchy course you know that CPUs move memory in whole cache lines, never single bytes.

This course asks the GPU version of that question: when a warp of 32 threads loads data, what actually moves, and how much of it is wasted?

The question matters because most kernels do little arithmetic per byte. An element-wise add reads two floats and writes one for a single addition, so its speed is set by how fast bytes arrive, not by how fast the SM can add. The CUDA Best Practices Guide puts coalescing of global memory accesses at **High Priority** for exactly this reason.

CUDA exposes several memory spaces. Each has a **scope** (who can see it) and a **location** (on the SM chip or off it in device memory):

- **Registers**: private to one thread, on the SM, allocated by the compiler.
- **Shared memory**: visible to all threads of one block, on the SM. It is a scratchpad you manage yourself, and it uses the same physical storage as the L1 cache.
- **L1 cache**: one per SM, caches global and local accesses.
- **L2 cache**: on the GPU, shared by all SMs.
- **Global memory** (also called device memory): the large DRAM visible to every thread and to the host, allocated with `cudaMalloc`. On data-center GPUs this DRAM is HBM (high-bandwidth memory).

blocks.title: Where data lives on an NVIDIA H100

scenes.caption: Two SMs of the many on the chip. Registers, shared memory and L1 sit inside each SM; L2 and HBM are shared by the whole GPU.
H100 sizes from NVIDIA's Hopper documents: 64K 32-bit registers (256 KB) and 256 KB of combined L1 and shared memory per SM, a 50 MB L2, and 80 GB of HBM3.
A global load that misses everywhere travels HBM to L2 to L1 to a register. Every hop is shared by many warps, so wasted bytes on this path cost everyone bandwidth.
Shared memory is filled and read by explicit instructions in your kernel. Threads of one block use it to exchange data without a trip to HBM.
When a thread needs more registers than it gets, the compiler spills values to local memory. Local memory is per thread in scope but lives in device memory, behind the same caches as global.

blocks.md:
The H100 SXM5 numbers, from NVIDIA's Hopper architecture post and the Hopper tuning guide: 132 SMs; per SM, 65,536 32-bit registers (256 KB) with at most 255 registers per thread; 256 KB of combined L1, texture cache and shared memory per SM, of which up to 228 KB can be shared memory (227 KB usable by a single block); a 50 MB L2; and 80 GB of HBM3 that the tuning guide rates at up to 3 TB/s.

Notice the shape: the whole GPU holds 132 x 256 KB = 33,792 KB of registers, about two thirds the size of the 50 MB L2, yet every byte a kernel works on still has to arrive from HBM through that one shared L2.

Shared memory and L1 are carved from the same storage. On Hopper you choose the split (the *carveout*) with `cudaFuncSetAttribute` and `cudaFuncAttributePreferredSharedMemoryCarveout`; supported shared memory sizes are 0, 8, 16, 32, 64, 100, 132, 164, 196 and 228 KB per SM. Static `__shared__` arrays are limited to 48 KB per block, and larger allocations must be dynamic with an explicit opt-in.

**Local memory is not local to the chip.** The word refers to scope (one thread), not location. Spilled registers, large per-thread arrays and arrays indexed with values the compiler cannot resolve at compile time all go to local memory, which has the latency and bandwidth of global memory.

Speed and capacity trade off at every level: registers and shared memory are on the SM and fast but small, L2 is shared by all SMs, and HBM is large but far away. Kernel design is mostly about making each byte fetched from HBM count.

blocks.question: A kernel declares `float buf[64];` per thread and indexes it with `buf[idx[i]]`, where `idx` is read from global memory. Where is `buf` most likely stored?
options: In registers, because it is declared inside the kernel
In shared memory, because it is an array
In local memory, which physically lives in device memory
In the L2 cache, which is reserved for per-thread arrays
blocks.explain: The CUDA Programming Guide lists arrays indexed with values the compiler cannot determine as constants among the variables likely placed in local memory. Local memory is thread-scoped but resides in device memory, so accesses cost like global memory, though they go through the caches.

blocks.question: Which level of the hierarchy is shared by every SM on the GPU?
options: Shared memory
The L2 cache
The register file
The L1 cache
blocks.explain: Shared memory, L1 and registers are per SM. The Programming Guide describes L2 as located on the device and shared among all the SMs, which is why one kernel's wasteful traffic can slow every other SM.

lessons.title: How a warp's 32 addresses become 32-byte sectors

blocks.md: When a warp executes one load instruction, each of its 32 threads supplies an address. The hardware does not fetch 32 separate words. It looks at all 32 addresses together and **coalesces** them: it works out the smallest set of memory transactions that covers every requested byte.

The unit of that transaction is a **sector**: an aligned 32-byte chunk of memory. The CUDA Programming Guide states that global memory is accessed via 32-byte memory transactions. Above sectors sit **cache lines**: NVIDIA's Nsight Compute documentation describes L1 and L2 lines as 128 bytes, made of four sectors, and data is tracked per sector within a line.

The rule for compute capability 6.0 and newer, from the Best Practices Guide: a warp's accesses coalesce into as many transactions as the number of 32-byte segments needed to serve all its threads.

blocks.caption: a_t is the byte address thread t asks for. Count the distinct 32-byte segments touched; efficiency is the share of fetched bytes the warp actually uses.

blocks.prompt: Thread t of a warp reads the 4-byte float `x[t]`, and `x` starts on a 32-byte boundary. How many sectors does the warp request?
blocks.reveal: **4.** The warp asks for 32 x 4 = 128 contiguous bytes. Bytes 0 to 31 are sector 0, 32 to 63 sector 1, and so on, so threads 0 to 7 share sector 0, threads 8 to 15 share sector 1, and four sectors cover everything. Every fetched byte is used: 128 / (32 x 4) = 100% efficiency. This is the guide's example of perfectly coalesced access.

blocks.title: Which 32-byte sector each thread's 4-byte load hits

scenes.caption: Unit stride: thread t reads byte 4t. Eight neighbors share each sector, so the warp needs sectors 0 to 3: 4 sectors for 128 useful bytes, 100% efficiency.
Reversed: thread t reads float 31 minus t. The order inside the warp does not matter, only which segments are touched: still 4 sectors.
Stride 2: thread t reads float 2t, so each sector holds only 4 requested floats. 8 sectors are fetched for 128 useful bytes: 50% efficiency.
Stride 8 (32 bytes apart): every thread lands in its own sector. 32 sectors, 1024 bytes moved for 128 used: 12.5%, the guide's worst case.
All 32 threads read the same float: one sector serves the whole warp. Few sectors is good, but here only 4 distinct bytes are useful.

blocks.md: Two consequences follow. First, coalescing is about the *set* of segments, not the order of threads: the Programming Guide says access is coalesced as long as threads touch the same 32-byte segments in some linear or permuted way. Second, once threads are 32 bytes or more apart, the damage stops growing because each thread already has a private sector. That is the worst case of 32 transactions per request.

blocks.title: Sectors and efficiency per warp load, 4-byte floats

scenes.caption: Sectors per warp request, computed by counting distinct 32-byte segments for float x[s x t]. Sectors grow as 4s until they hit 32 at stride 8.
The same counts as the percentage of fetched bytes the warp uses: 128 bytes divided by 32 times the sector count. Beyond stride 8 it stays at 12.5%.

blocks.md: Element size changes the numbers but not the rule. If each thread loads a 16-byte `float4` at unit stride, the warp requests 512 contiguous bytes, which is 16 sectors, all fully used. If each thread loads an 8-byte `double`, unit stride needs 8 sectors. Efficiency stays at 100% in both cases because neighbors still share every sector.

In 2D kernels, the trap is index order. `threadIdx.x` varies fastest within a warp, so it must index the contiguous dimension. In a row-major array, `a[row * ld + col]` with `col` built from `threadIdx.x` is coalesced; the same expression with `row` built from `threadIdx.x` puts consecutive threads `ld` elements apart.

**Misconception:** coalescing requires thread k to read element k. It does not. The Programming Guide notes that permuted access within the same 32-byte segments is just as good. What matters is the ratio of bytes used to bytes transferred.
Count distinct 32-byte sectors per warp request. 4 for 32 consecutive floats is ideal; 32 is the worst case and wastes 87.5% of the traffic.

blocks.question: A row-major `float` matrix has `ld = 4096` columns. A kernel with 32 x 32 blocks computes `int r = blockIdx.y*32 + threadIdx.x; int c = blockIdx.x*32 + threadIdx.y;` and reads `a[r*ld + c]`. How many sectors does each warp load request?
options: 4, because the warp reads 32 floats
8, because the matrix is large
1, because all threads share c
32, because consecutive threads are 4096 floats apart
blocks.explain: Within a warp threadIdx.y is fixed and threadIdx.x runs 0 to 31, so it is r that varies. Consecutive threads are ld = 4096 floats (16 KB) apart, each in its own sector: 32 sectors per request and 12.5% efficiency. Swapping which index uses threadIdx.x fixes it.

blocks.question: Each thread of a warp reads an 8-byte `double` at `d[t]`, starting at an aligned address. How many sectors are requested, and what fraction of the fetched bytes is used?
options: 4 sectors, 100%
8 sectors, 100%
8 sectors, 50%
32 sectors, 25%
blocks.explain: The warp asks for 32 x 8 = 256 contiguous bytes, which is exactly 8 sectors of 32 bytes. Every fetched byte is requested by some thread, so efficiency is 256 / 256 = 100%.

blocks.md: Sector counting also explains misalignment. Memory from `cudaMalloc` is aligned to at least 256 bytes, so a warp reading 32 consecutive floats from the start of an array hits exactly 4 sectors. Shift the start by one float and the same 128 bytes straddle a sector boundary at each end.

blocks.title: Offset copies: sectors touched per warp

scenes.caption: Offset 0: thread t reads float t. Sectors 0 to 3, so 4 sectors.
Offset 1 float: thread t reads float t+1. Thread 31 spills into sector 4, so the warp fetches 5 sectors for 128 useful bytes, 80% efficiency.
Offset 8 floats (32 bytes): sectors 1 to 4. The range crosses a 128-byte line boundary, yet it is still only 4 sectors, because the transaction unit is the sector.

blocks.prompt: The Best Practices Guide runs `offsetCopy`, `odata[xid] = idata[xid]` with `xid` shifted by an offset, on a Tesla V100. Aligned copies reach about 790 GB/s. Offsets that are not a multiple of 8 floats need 5 sectors instead of 4. What bandwidth would you expect, and what was measured?
blocks.reveal: The sector model predicts 4/5 of 790, about 632 GB/s. The guide reports roughly **9/10** instead, about 711 GB/s. The difference is caching: the extra sector one warp fetches is the first sector the next warp needs, so adjacent warps reuse it from cache instead of going back to DRAM. Caches soften misalignment, but only when neighbors actually reuse the over-fetched data.

blocks.md: Strides are harder for caches to rescue. With `strideCopy`, which reads `idata[xid * stride]`, a stride of 2 makes each warp load 8 L2 sectors on the V100 and wastes half of every one of them. The Best Practices Guide shows effective bandwidth falling as the stride grows until each warp loads 32 sectors.

To compare kernels you need a number. **Theoretical bandwidth** comes from the hardware: the V100 has HBM2 at a memory clock of 877 MHz with a 4096-bit interface, transferring on both clock edges. **Effective bandwidth** comes from your kernel: bytes it logically reads and writes, divided by measured time.

blocks.tex: BW_{\text{theory}} = \frac{0.877 \times 10^{9} \times (4096/8) \times 2}{10^{9}} = 898 \text{ GB/s}, \qquad BW_{\text{eff}} = \frac{(B_r + B_w)/10^{9}}{\text{time in s}}
blocks.caption: From the Best Practices Guide. Count only the bytes your algorithm needs, so wasted sector bytes show up as lost effective bandwidth. Use the same divisor (10^9 or 1024^3) on both sides.

blocks.md: A worked example. Copying a 2048 x 2048 float matrix reads and writes $2048^2 \times 4$ bytes each, so $B_r + B_w = 33{,}554{,}432$ bytes, about 0.0336 GB. At 790 GB/s that takes about 42.5 microseconds. Make the reads stride 8 and every warp drags in 8 times more sectors than it uses; the model below shows how hard that caps you.

blocks.title: Simple model: useful bandwidth vs stride

scenes.caption: V100 theoretical 898 GB/s. If every fetched sector comes from DRAM, useful bandwidth is peak divided by sectors-per-useful-sector: 449 GB/s at stride 2, 112 GB/s from stride 8 on.
Raise the peak to 3000 GB/s, the H100 SXM5 figure in NVIDIA's tuning guide. The curve scales but keeps its shape: a faster GPU does not fix a wasteful access pattern.
Simplified: this ignores cache reuse between warps (which helped offsetCopy) and other limits. Treat it as an upper bound for streaming data that is touched once.

blocks.md: Do not guess sector counts in real code: Nsight Compute's memory tables report a Sectors/Req ratio for global loads and stores. Its documentation gives 4 as the ideal for 32 threads each loading an aligned 32-bit value, and reads 32 as every thread needing its own sector.

**Misconception:** the L1 cache makes access patterns irrelevant. Caches help when nearby warps reuse what was over-fetched, as with small misalignments. A large stride over data read once gets no reuse, and every unused byte still crosses the DRAM interface.

blocks.question: A kernel reads `x[i * 4]` (floats) for consecutive `i` across a warp, and each element is used once. What fraction of fetched bytes is useful, ignoring cache reuse?
blocks.explain: Threads are 16 bytes apart, so each 32-byte sector holds 2 requested floats: 16 sectors per warp for 128 useful bytes. 128 / (16 x 32) = 25%.

blocks.question: Why did the V100 offsetCopy measurement lose only about 10% instead of the 20% the sector count predicts?
options: The V100 hardware realigns misaligned addresses for free
cudaMalloc pads arrays so that offsets never cross a sector
Adjacent warps reuse the over-fetched boundary sectors from cache
The kernel was limited by arithmetic, not memory
blocks.explain: Each warp's fifth sector is the next warp's first. The Best Practices Guide attributes the 9/10 result to adjacent warps reusing cache lines their neighbors fetched.

lessons.title: Shared memory banks and bank conflicts

blocks.md: Shared memory is the fix for many bad global access patterns: load data coalesced, then reorder it on chip. But shared memory has its own access rule. It is divided into **32 banks**, and successive 32-bit words map to successive banks. Each bank delivers 32 bits per clock cycle.

blocks.caption: a is the byte offset within shared memory. Word 0 is in bank 0, word 31 in bank 31, word 32 back in bank 0.

blocks.md: If the 32 threads of a warp hit 32 different banks, the access completes at full speed. If several threads hit **different words in the same bank**, that is a **bank conflict**: the hardware splits the request into as many conflict-free requests as needed, and bandwidth drops by that factor. An n-way conflict costs n passes. Threads reading the **same word** do not conflict: the word is broadcast to all of them.

blocks.title: Bank hit by each thread for word index s x t

scenes.caption: Stride 1: thread t reads word t, banks 0 to 31, each once. One pass, no conflict.
Stride 2: thread t reads word 2t. Only the 16 even banks are used, each by two threads asking for different words: a 2-way conflict, 2 passes.
Stride 3: word 3t. Because 3 shares no factor with 32, the 32 banks come out as a permutation of 0 to 31. No conflict.
Stride 32: word 32t. Every thread is in bank 0 asking for a different word: a 32-way conflict, 32 serialized passes.
All threads read word 0. Same bank, but the same word, so it is broadcast in one pass. Not a conflict.

blocks.prompt: Why are stride 1 and stride 3 conflict-free but stride 2 is not? Can you state the rule for any stride s?
blocks.reveal: Thread t hits bank $(s t) \bmod 32$. Those values repeat every $32/\gcd(s,32)$ threads, so each used bank is hit by $\gcd(s,32)$ different words. The conflict degree is $\gcd(s,32)$: 1 for any odd stride, 2 for stride 2, 4 for stride 4, 32 for stride 32. A script checking every stride from 1 to 64 agrees.

blocks.title: Conflict degree (passes per warp access) by word stride

scenes.caption: Computed by counting distinct words per bank. Stride 33 behaves like stride 1 because 33 mod 32 is 1: this is the trick behind padding.

blocks.md: Where does stride 32 come from in practice? A 2D tile. In `__shared__ float tile[32][32];` the element `tile[r][c]` is word `32r + c`, so its bank is just `c`. A warp that reads across a row hits 32 banks. A warp that reads down a column, `tile[threadIdx.x][k]`, hits bank `k` 32 times.

blocks.title: Bank of each element, top-left 8 x 8 of a tile

scenes.caption: float tile[32][32]: bank equals the column index, so every row has the same colors. Shown is the 8 x 8 corner; the pattern continues to 32.
A warp reading row 0 touches 32 different banks: conflict-free.
A warp reading column 0 touches bank 0 in every row: a 32-way conflict.
Pad to float tile[32][33]: element (r, c) is word 33r + c, bank (r + c) mod 32. Each row is shifted by one bank.
Column 0 now hits banks 0, 1, 2 and onward, all different. Rows are still conflict-free. One unused word per row bought this.

blocks.md: The padding costs little: a 32 x 33 float tile is 4,224 bytes instead of 4,096, about 3.1% more shared memory, and the extra column is never read. Both the CUDA Programming Guide and NVIDIA's transpose post use exactly this fix.

**Padding by any amount does not work.** The conflict degree is $\gcd(\text{row width}, 32)$. A row width of 33 gives 1, but a width of 34 gives a 2-way conflict and 48 gives 16-way. Pick an odd width.
Bank = word index mod 32. Different words in one bank serialize; the same word broadcasts. For column access to a 2D tile, make the row width odd.

blocks.question: You pad a tile to `__shared__ float t[32][34];` and a warp reads `t[threadIdx.x][5]`. What happens?
options: No conflict, because the tile is padded
A 2-way bank conflict
A 32-way bank conflict
A broadcast, because every thread uses column 5
blocks.explain: Thread i reads word 34i + 5, bank (2i + 5) mod 32. Only 16 banks are used, each by two different words, so gcd(34, 32) = 2 passes. Odd widths like 33 avoid it.

blocks.question: All 32 threads of a warp read `s[7]` from a shared float array. How many passes does the access need?
options: 32, because every thread uses bank 7
16, because pairs of threads share a pass
1, because the word is broadcast
2, because reads of one bank are paired
blocks.explain: A bank conflict needs different addresses in the same bank. Here every thread asks for the same word, which the hardware broadcasts in a single pass.

lessons.title: Case study: one matrix transpose, three kernels

blocks.md: A matrix transpose combines everything so far. It does no arithmetic, so a good transpose should run as fast as a plain copy. Mark Harris's NVIDIA post *An Efficient Matrix Transpose in CUDA C/C++* builds it in steps on a 1024 x 1024 float matrix, using 32 x 8 thread blocks where each block handles a 32 x 32 tile (each thread moves 4 elements).

blocks.caption: The naive kernel from the NVIDIA post. Reads walk along a row; writes walk down a column.

blocks.prompt: For one warp of `transposeNaive` (32 threads with consecutive threadIdx.x), how many sectors does the read need, and how many does the write need?
blocks.reveal: The read `idata[(y+j)*width + x]` has `x` varying, so it is 32 consecutive floats: **4 sectors**. The write `odata[x*width + ...]` puts consecutive threads `width = 1024` floats (4,096 bytes) apart: **32 sectors**, 12.5% efficiency. The copy kernel, identical except for the write index, needs 4 sectors for both.

blocks.title: Staging a tile through shared memory

scenes.caption: Naive: reading rows is coalesced, but the write goes straight to a column of odata. Each warp write costs 32 sectors.
Tiled: each warp reads a row of idata (4 sectors) and stores it as a row of the shared tile, which is conflict-free.
Barrier: threads will next read elements other threads wrote, so every warp must finish its stores first.
Each warp reads a column of the tile and writes it as a row of odata: 4 sectors per warp. With a 32-wide tile this column read is a 32-way conflict; width 33 removes it.

blocks.title: One warp (threadIdx.y = 0) through the final kernel

scenes.caption: The padded tile: 33 floats per row so column reads spread over all banks.
Load, j = 0: threads read idata[y*1024 + x] for x = 0 to 31, contiguous, and store into tile[0][x], banks 0 to 31.
The loop repeats for j = 8, 16, 24, so this 32 x 8 block fills all 32 rows of the tile.
Wait for all warps of the block before anyone reads the tile.
Swap the block offsets so the tile lands at its transposed position in odata.
Store, j = 0: thread x reads tile[x][0], word 33x, bank x mod 32: no conflict. It writes odata at consecutive addresses: 4 sectors.
Same line with TILE_DIM+1 replaced by TILE_DIM: word 32x, always bank 0. Global traffic is unchanged; the shared read becomes a 32-way conflict.

blocks.title: Measured effective bandwidth in the NVIDIA transpose post

scenes.caption: Tesla M2050, ECC on. Naive reaches 18.8 GB/s, 18% of copy. Staging through shared memory lifts it to 51.3; padding the tile reaches 99.5.
Tesla K20c, ECC on: 55.3, then 97.6, then 144.3 GB/s, about 95% of the 152.3 GB/s shared-memory copy. Same ranking on a newer GPU.

blocks.md:
Turn those into time. A 1024 x 1024 float transpose reads and writes 4 MiB each, $B_r + B_w = 8{,}388{,}608$ bytes. On the K20c that is about 151.7 microseconds naive versus 58.1 microseconds with no bank conflicts; on the M2050, 446.2 versus 84.3. The kernels move identical data; only the access pattern changed.

The Best Practices Guide tells the same story on a Tesla V100 with $C = AA^T$: strided global reads give 12.8 GB/s, coalesced reads through a shared tile give 140.2 GB/s, and padding that tile to remove bank conflicts gives 199.4 GB/s.

These measurements come from older GPUs (Fermi and Kepler in the post, Volta in the guide). Absolute numbers on a current GPU will differ, and larger caches can hide some waste. The sector and bank rules they illustrate are the ones the current CUDA guides still document.

The NVIDIA post's conclusion: coalescing global memory accesses is by far the most critical step. Use shared memory to turn strided global access into coalesced access, then check the shared access for bank conflicts.

blocks.question: In `transposeCoalesced` (tile declared `[32][32]`), which access suffers the bank conflict?
options: The global read of idata, because it is strided
The store into tile[threadIdx.y+j][threadIdx.x]
The global write of odata, because it is transposed
The read of tile[threadIdx.x][threadIdx.y+j]
blocks.explain: The store walks along a tile row (word 32 row + x, banks 0 to 31). The read walks down a column: word 32x + k for x = 0 to 31, all in bank k, a 32-way conflict. Both global accesses are coalesced.

blocks.question: A teammate drops `__syncthreads()` from the tiled transpose because "each thread only touches its own data." What is wrong?
options: Nothing; the barrier only affects performance
Threads read tile elements written by other warps, so they may read before those writes happen
Without the barrier the global writes become uncoalesced
The barrier is needed only when the tile is padded
blocks.explain: Thread (x, y) stores tile[y+j][x] but later reads tile[x][y+j], an element another thread, often in another warp, stored. The NVIDIA transpose post requires `__syncthreads()` because threads write different data to odata than they read from idata, and the CUDA guide says synchronization is necessary when threads of a block share shared memory addresses.
